Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 5 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#c32-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** Two versions of a claim cite the same evidence. One uses familiar wording; the other uses unfamiliar jargon. Which reader response illustrates an effect of processing fluency?

A) Giving a version more credibility because most colleagues agree with it
B) Giving a version more credibility because a recent personal experience supports it
C) Giving the familiar version more credibility because it feels easier to read
D) Giving a version more credibility because it supports an existing opinion
E) Giving a version more credibility because a trusted specialist endorses it

:::

::: {#c32-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** A clearly explained proposal is called voluntary, but declining it reduces promotion prospects. Which aspect of message design is directly contradicted?

A) Comprehensibility of the proposed action
B) Numerical precision of the forecast
C) Representativeness of a supporting sample
D) Visibility of the message's author
E) Practical freedom to refuse

:::

::: {#c32-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** A survey finds that users of a fitness app exercise more than nonusers. Which additional finding would most strengthen a causal claim about offering the app?

A) The exercise difference is larger among people who use the app more frequently.
B) Random assignment to app access increases exercise relative to a comparison group.
C) Users and nonusers give similar ratings to the importance of healthy living.
D) Users rate the app as helpful when explaining why they exercise regularly.
E) The same exercise difference appears in a larger survey conducted the following year.

:::

::: {#c32-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A forecast is sensitive to future energy prices. Which communication makes that uncertainty useful for a decision?

A) Add “results may vary” without explaining why.
B) Remove the energy-price assumption from the message.
C) Show the assumed prices and how plausible alternatives change the recommendation.
D) Report more decimal places for the central forecast.
E) Replace the range with the most optimistic possible price.

:::

::: {#c32-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A well-designed study finds that a program reduces failures from 6 per 100 to 4 per 100 over one year. Which summary preserves the absolute and relative changes?

A) Two fewer failures per 100; about a 33% relative reduction.
B) Six fewer failures per 100; a 50% relative reduction.
C) Two fewer failures per 100; about a 67% relative reduction.
D) Two fewer failures per 100; a 2% relative reduction.
E) Four fewer failures per 100; about a 33% relative reduction.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-c32)

::: {#answers-c32 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: C.**

- **A. Giving a version more credibility because most colleagues agree with it (Incorrect)** This relies on social influence rather than the ease of reading the claim.
- **B. Giving a version more credibility because a recent personal experience supports it (Incorrect)** This relies on accessible supporting experience rather than how easily the wording is processed.
- **C. Giving the familiar version more credibility because it feels easier to read (Correct)** Ease of processing can influence perceived credibility even when the evidence is unchanged.
- **D. Giving a version more credibility because it supports an existing opinion (Incorrect)** This reflects belief-consistent evaluation rather than processing fluency.
- **E. Giving a version more credibility because a trusted specialist endorses it (Incorrect)** This relies on source credibility rather than ease of processing.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 1](#c32-01).

**Question 2: E.**

- **A. Comprehensibility of the proposed action (Incorrect)** The stem states that it is clearly explained.
- **B. Numerical precision of the forecast (Incorrect)** No forecast precision is specified.
- **C. Representativeness of a supporting sample (Incorrect)** No sample or empirical support is described.
- **D. Visibility of the message's author (Incorrect)** The problem concerns consequences of refusal, not source identification.
- **E. Practical freedom to refuse (Correct)** The material penalty makes the stated voluntariness misleading.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 2](#c32-02).

**Question 3: B.**

- **A. The exercise difference is larger among people who use the app more frequently. (Incorrect)** More motivated exercisers may use the app more often, so a dose association does not remove selection.
- **B. Random assignment to app access increases exercise relative to a comparison group. (Correct)** Random assignment addresses selection into access and tests the effect of offering the app.
- **C. Users and nonusers give similar ratings to the importance of healthy living. (Incorrect)** Similarity on one reported characteristic does not establish comparability on other causes of exercise.
- **D. Users rate the app as helpful when explaining why they exercise regularly. (Incorrect)** Users' interpretations may suggest a mechanism but do not isolate a causal effect.
- **E. The same exercise difference appears in a larger survey conducted the following year. (Incorrect)** Replication and precision do not by themselves remove confounding.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 3](#c32-03).

**Question 4: C.**

- **A. Add “results may vary” without explaining why. (Incorrect)** A blanket qualifier does not reveal the decision-relevant uncertainty.
- **B. Remove the energy-price assumption from the message. (Incorrect)** Hiding the assumption makes evaluation harder.
- **C. Show the assumed prices and how plausible alternatives change the recommendation. (Correct)** This links uncertainty to the action it could alter.
- **D. Report more decimal places for the central forecast. (Incorrect)** Precision does not explain sensitivity.
- **E. Replace the range with the most optimistic possible price. (Incorrect)** Selecting a favorable value conceals the sensitivity.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 4](#c32-04).

**Question 5: A.**

- **A. Two fewer failures per 100; about a 33% relative reduction. (Correct)** The absolute drop is 2/100 and the relative drop is 2/6.
- **B. Six fewer failures per 100; a 50% relative reduction. (Incorrect)** Neither quantity follows from the change from six to four.
- **C. Two fewer failures per 100; about a 67% relative reduction. (Incorrect)** 4/6 is the remaining proportion, not the fraction removed.
- **D. Two fewer failures per 100; a 2% relative reduction. (Incorrect)** Two percentage points is not a 2% relative reduction from six.
- **E. Four fewer failures per 100; about a 33% relative reduction. (Incorrect)** Four is the new rate, not the reduction.

Review: [Chapter 32](../chapters/32-message-design.qmd). [Back to question 5](#c32-05).

:::
